Chapter 8: Inheritance, Merit, and the Myth of Equal Opportunity
Let’s talk about a story we’ve all heard—maybe you’ve even told it to yourself. It’s that idea that anyone can make it, if they just work hard enough. Sounds inspiring, right?
But real life, as you might’ve noticed, is a little messier. The truth is, inheritance—the wealth you’re born into, the connections you inherit, the family background you can’t change—still plays a huge role, even in places where merit is supposed to matter most.
Picture this: a young graduate, ready to take on the world, steps into her first job hunt. She’s smart, she’s ambitious, and she’s not afraid of hard work. But soon, she realizes that some doors just swing open for others. Maybe it’s because their parents can pay for fancy internships, or they know people who can pull a few strings, or they don’t have to stress about student loans. Suddenly, that dream of equal opportunity feels a little out of reach.
And here’s something to pay attention to—inheritance isn’t just about money. It’s about all those subtle advantages that shape a life. Think about the schools you go to, the neighborhoods you grow up in, or the networks you build from the time you’re a kid. These things add up. Over the years, they can make it so much easier for some people to get ahead, while others always feel like they’re playing catch-up.
Most folks don’t really notice the invisible hand of inheritance at work. What they do see are the outcomes—a sense that some people always seem to land on their feet, no matter what, while others keep struggling, no matter how hard they push. The numbers back this up, too. In a lot of countries, more and more wealth is being passed down from one generation to the next. If we’re not careful, we could end up right back in a world where your birth matters more than your effort, and the promise of meritocracy is just talk.
So, what can we do about it? Some folks suggest raising inheritance taxes, making education more accessible, or finding ways to break down those stubborn barriers. Others worry that we might stifle ambition, or that we’re punishing people for their success. It's a tough debate, and it’s far from settled.
But here’s the key takeaway—the society we build depends on how we balance merit and inheritance. It’s not just an abstract argument; it shapes real lives, including yours and mine.
